questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Wronskian Using Abel's Identity
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+5y=0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(1)=2.$ What is $W(4)?$

$W(4)=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=-3.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=3W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =3W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =3\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int 3\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =3x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{3x} \\ W & =C{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =C{e}^{3\cdot 1} \\ 2 & =C{e}^{3} \\ C & =2{e}^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=2{e}^{-3}{e}^{3x}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(4) & =2{e}^{-3}{e}^{3\cdot 4}=2{e}^{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{2}{x}{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(1)=6.$ What is $W(3)?$

$W(3)=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{2}{x}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{2}{x}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{2}{x}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{2}{x}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{x}^{-2} \\ W & =\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(1)=6$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =\frac{C}{{1}^{2}} \\ 6 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(3) & =\frac{6}{{3}^{2}}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
